text: A 1 TB file holds 10^12 bytes, but a 4-byte integer only reaches about 2.1 billion (signed) or 4.3 billion (unsigned). Byte offsets into the file must therefore be 64-bit (8-byte) integers. With 8-byte offsets the 170,000-word index is still only a few MB.
why: Fixes the one number in the sizing that would not work in code.

text: Average word length depends on what you count. In running text it is about 4.8 letters, because short words like 'the' repeat; across distinct words it is about 7.6 letters (Norvig's Google Books counts). A dictionary index stores distinct words, so the larger figure applies.
why: Shows learners how to choose the right average for a back-of-envelope estimate.

text: S3 GetObject takes a standard HTTP Range header: for example, 'Range: bytes=0-9' returns only the first 10 bytes, and the response carries a Content-Range header. That call is what makes pointed reads into one big S3 object possible.
why: Names the exact API mechanism behind the design.

text: A server can guard against reading a replaced file. It sends the ranged GET with If-Match set to the ETag its index was built from, and S3 returns 412 Precondition Failed instead of bytes if the object changed. The server can then reload its index rather than return garbage.
why: Gives a concrete fix for the garbage-read failure mode.

text: On S3, overwriting a key is atomic: a reader that races with the upload gets 'either the old data or the new data, but never partial or corrupt data'. The danger of a same-path upload is the stale index offsets, not a half-written file.
why: Corrects the intuition that an upload in progress exposes a partial file.

text: A 1 TB dictionary cannot be uploaded in one request: a single S3 PUT is limited to 5 GB, so large files use multipart upload. As of October 2026, multipart allows up to 10,000 parts of 5 MiB to 5 GiB each, and objects up to about 50 TB (48.8 TiB).
why: The update job has to upload a 1 TB file; this is how it is actually done.

text: Redis Pub/Sub is at-most-once: if a subscriber cannot handle a message, for example because of a network disconnect, 'the message is forever lost'. An API server that restarts at the wrong moment would miss the update event. Redis Streams persist messages if you need stronger delivery.
why: A concrete reliability reason, beyond complexity, to prefer the deployment trigger.

text: AWS documents S3 first-byte latency of roughly 100-200 ms, and at least 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix. That is why serving every lookup straight from S3 is slow, and why real systems cache hot entries.
why: Puts numbers on 'how costly is one S3 call per request'.

text: SQLite is a real-world example of this portability: 'A database in SQLite is a single disk file'. The format is cross-platform, so a database created on one machine can be copied to and used on another architecture.
why: Shows the one-file portability requirement is a real design goal of widely used software.

text: The ZIP format itself is a one-file container with an index. A central directory near the end of the archive records, for every member, the offset of its local header, so a reader can seek straight to one file without unpacking the rest.
why: Same header-plus-index idea as the dictionary file, in a format everyone uses.

text: Athena does not index CSV rows; it scans the files and charges per TB scanned. To make Athena queries cheaper and faster, compress the data, partition it, and convert it to a columnar format like Parquet so Athena reads only the needed columns.
why: Corrects the 'Athena builds an index' impression and gives the real optimisation levers.

text: AWS uses three storage terms. Block storage (Amazon EBS) is a disk-like volume attached to an instance. File storage (Amazon EFS) is a shared network file system, and object storage (Amazon S3) holds whole objects fetched over HTTP by key; the dictionary file on S3 is object storage.
why: Gives the correct vocabulary for an interview answer.

text: With S3 Versioning, each upload to the same key gets a unique version ID, and GetObject can request a specific version with the versionId parameter. Storing the version ID next to the path in meta.json would let every server keep reading exactly the version its index was built from.
why: Shows how the S3-specific route maps onto the meta.json design.

text: On AWS, an EC2 Auto Scaling instance refresh provides this out of the box. The rolling strategy replaces instances in batches, and with a minimum healthy percentage of 100 percent it launches new instances before terminating old ones, so capacity never drops.
why: Names a concrete managed feature for 'trigger a rolling deployment'.

text: JSON Lines (one JSON value per line) is the usual fix when JSON must hold many records: it 'may be processed one record at a time', so readers stream it line by line instead of parsing one giant document. It still has no index, so a lookup is still a scan.
why: A common real-world format learners will meet; clarifies what it does and does not solve.

text: A Lucene index is made of segments, each 'a fully independent index', plus a segments_N commit file. The optional compound format packs one segment's files into a single .cfs file.
why: Corrects the 'one Lucene index is one file' comparison.

text: HDFS supports the same pointed read: its input streams offer seek() and positioned reads from a given byte offset. The offset-index design therefore also works on HDFS.
why: Backs the teacher's remark that HDFS supports random reads.
